plain_language: A local AI coding model now runs nearly 90% faster on a Mac, no new hardware. A firm serving open models raised $800M. A chip startup kept itself independent instead of selling.
findings:
Today's cycle has no single forcing event; instead its coherence runs along one theme, the economics of running AI outside the biggest clouds, and each of three fresh predictions plants a flag in it. The densest technical signal is Ollama 0.31, shipped July 1, which turns on multi-token prediction by default for Gemma 4 on Apple Silicon and reports the model generating tokens nearly 90% faster across a coding-agent benchmark with byte-identical output, plus an upstreamed small-batch MLX matmul kernel that makes Gemma 4's largest matmuls 2x to 2.5x faster on an M5 Max with nvfp4 and is reusable by any MLX model. That is the origin evidence for the fresh 'local-LLM runtimes ship in-model speculative decoding on by default' forecast (July 5), scoring maximum relevance because it ships as a default rather than a tuning flag, and because coding agents call the model continuously over highly predictable code the accepted drafts compound over a session. The same release sharpens the 'quantized-by-default serving lands as the OSS inference baseline' thesis (June 30) from the local-runtime side, reinforces the 'launch-day vLLM/SGLang plus Ollama support becomes the open-weight release bar' norm (July 2) via its Claude Code and opencode auto-install hooks, and revives the dormant 'consumer-GPU coding agents displace cloud-only APIs for 30% of devs' longshot (April 26) by narrowing the on-device-versus-hosted gap exactly where that thesis lives. The remaining gap is honest: no second mainstream local runtime, LM Studio, an llama.cpp desktop, MLX-LM, or vLLM's local mode, has yet flipped speculative decoding to the default path.

The second load-bearing thread is capital moving one layer down the AI stack, into the open-model inference tier, and it too anchors a fresh prediction. Together AI announced an $800 million Series C at an $8.3 billion post-money valuation on July 1, a 2.5x step-up from its February 2025 round, led by Aramco's Prosperity7 with NVIDIA, Vista, and General Catalyst participating, and its lead investor framed the company, a neocloud serving DeepSeek, Nemotron, MiniMax, and Kimi at a fraction of closed-model cost, as headed toward the public markets. That is the origin evidence for the fresh 'open-model inference neocloud files a public-listing step' forecast (July 5), it adds a same-direction data point to the 'OpenAI files a public-listing step with a US-government stake' backdrop (July 4), and it revives the dormant 'frontier AI lab files a public S-1 and prices its IPO' longshot (June 12) at the market-window level, now visible in the inference tier and framed as continuous with the labs' own IPO pull. The missing piece is a concrete disclosed step, a confidential or public S-1, rather than investor commentary.

The third thread is the non-GPU silicon layer being named and funded as its own category, and it carries a fresh prediction plus a revival across two reinforcing signals in one cycle. Stathera closed an oversubscribed $55 million Series B on June 30, led by Maverick Silicon with MediaTek and TXC participating, explicitly to fund a GEN3 platform for AI-data-center clocks, pitching MEMS DualMode timing as a roughly $1.5 billion cumulative synchronization opportunity through 2030 as accelerator clusters scale to tens of thousands of GPUs; in parallel, Tenstorrent's Jim Keller publicly denied the reported $8-10 billion Qualcomm buyout and reaffirmed an independent IPO-bridge and confidential-S-1 path, keeping a credible RISC-V accelerator-IP house standalone rather than folding into a mobile-SoC incumbent. Together they are the origin evidence for the fresh 'non-GPU AI-datacenter silicon draws standalone infrastructure funding' forecast (July 5), and the Tenstorrent leg alone touches the 'second hyperscaler names non-Nvidia data-center inference silicon' thesis (June 29), the 'inference-ASIC cohort gains a fourth named buyer-designed chip' thesis (June 25), and yesterday's 'second open-weight frontier model discloses non-NVIDIA ASIC training' forecast (July 4) by keeping the merchant non-NVIDIA supply pool alive, while reviving the dormant 'Tenstorrent S-1 anchors three-name AI-chip IPO set' longshot (May 24) at the intent-and-track level. Rounding out the day, the events calendar rolls AMD's MI400 Instinct series and Helios rack-scale system back to a general second-half watch item behind Geneva AI Week (July 6-10) and Hot Chips (August 23-25), so both 'AMD Instinct MI400 launches with a named ship, memory, or rack spec' (June 27) and 'AMD MI400 will market memory bandwidth over peak FLOPS' (July 2) recede from a firm near-term slot as their Q3 window narrows.
relation_to_my_preds:
The user's first standing prediction (malicious local LLM as malware plus zero-trust as the fundamental safeguard) gets little fresh evidence today, and it is worth stating that plainly rather than manufacturing a link. Yesterday's cycle was dominated by the agent-security axis, the two CVSS 9.8 zero-click Cursor sandbox-escape RCEs, but today's news carries no new agent-stack CVE, no MCP-server exploit, no model-registry supply-chain disclosure, and no procurement-gate or attestation instrument. The nearest adjacency is forward-looking calendar rather than substrate: the events roundup flags SecurityWeek's AI Risk Summit on August 11-12 and Black Hat plus DEF CON 34's AI Village in early August as the natural venues for agent-hijack and MCP-layer defense, and notes Zenity's AI Agent Security Summit series continuing on that beat. So the malicious-tooling threat and the zero-trust-attestation response both stand where yesterday left them, with the pressure decisive but quiet today and no signed-checkpoint, per-tenant-capability-gating, or federal-blocklist datapoint printing to move the thesis.

The user's second standing prediction (cloud APIs for advanced or frontier work plus local LLMs for daily, driven by SaaS price rises) is where today lands hardest, catching both poles of the bifurcation on the same day. The daily-local pole gets its strongest fresh substrate in a while from Ollama 0.31, whose default-on multi-token prediction makes Gemma 4 generate tokens nearly 90% faster on Apple Silicon with unchanged output and whose reusable MLX matmul kernel adds a 2x-2.5x speedup, the reporting concluding that on-device agentic throughput just closed a meaningful part of the gap to hosted inference without new hardware, which is exactly the local-daily leg's mechanism moving from aspiration to shipped default and reviving the dormant consumer-GPU-coding-agents thesis at the driver level. The cloud-and-capital pole lands through Together AI's $800 million Series C at $8.3 billion, a sovereign-scale Prosperity7-led round capitalizing the open-model inference neocloud as a durable platform tier serving DeepSeek, Nemotron, MiniMax, and Kimi below closed-model cost, alongside Fireworks and Baseten, and the non-NVIDIA accelerator economics harden underneath both poles as Tenstorrent's Keller rejects the $8-10 billion Qualcomm buyout to stay independent on an IPO bridge and Stathera raises $55 million for AI-datacenter timing silicon. The open question the thesis names, whether owned-GPU open-model inference can keep undercutting hosted frontier APIs on price while matching latency as open weights close the capability gap, is now precisely the competitive question this capital funds, so the day advances the bifurcation on substrate, capital, and hardware-supply legs at once.

The user's third standing prediction (RL/LLM-based forecasting performance improvement, with substrate, governance, and real-world-deployment legs hardening in parallel) gets only oblique contact today, and honesty requires marking it as a near-miss rather than a hit. Today's material is inference-and-capital economics, not training methodology: there is no long-horizon RL run, no router-only LoRA or ultra-long-context stability preprint, no MoE-backbone training recipe, and no autonomous-forecasting-agent result of the kind that lands squarely on the substrate leg. What today does add is a thin enabling-layer nudge, Ollama's default speculative decoding lowers the cost of running an agent that calls a model continuously over long, predictable rollouts, and the persistence of independent non-NVIDIA accelerator supply via Tenstorrent keeps the compute substrate an RL-forecasting stack could eventually train on from consolidating away, but neither is policy-gradient or forecasting evidence itself. The governance leg gets a faint adjacent flicker: Anthropic's Jack Clark taking a seat on the new UN AI for Good Commission alongside Jensen Huang, Andy Jassy, and Brad Smith at Geneva AI Week signals the multi-stakeholder attestation-and-standards venue this thesis tracks is convening, but no signed-skill-registry interop, NIST non-human-identity control profile, or physical-AI production-loop closure printed, so all three legs stay essentially where they were with only the faintest enabling-and-governance motion today.
